newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says Busang case no impact on policy.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says Busang case no impact on policy.

text.p: Indonesia said on Tuesday the Busang gold issue, a focus of world mining attention in recent months, would not affect the government's overall mining policy.

"The Busang case will not change the government's general mining policy, for the time being at least," Kuntoro Mangkusubroto, director general of mining in the Mines and Energy Ministry, told a news conference.
"The Busang case is a specific one," he said.
He said the goverment honoured contracts of work issued to foreign mining firms and their Indonesian partners to explore and develop properties.
"Once the contract of work is signed, all rules are nailed down for 30 years, plus two 10 years options to extend if wanted," he said.
Mining industry sources and analysts had expressed concern over the Busang case.

They said at one stage the government appeared to have cancelled approval for contracts of work for the small Canadian firm Bre-X Minerals Ltd to develop two areas of the huge Busang gold find in East Kalimantan province.
Last November, the government also told Bre-X it wanted the company to team up with Canada's Barrick Gold Corp to develop the find -- with the major stake going to Barrick.

On Tuesday, however, Mines and Energy Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana said the government had approved a new proposal from Bre-X under which the company would get 45 percent of the stake in the richest part of Busang, estimated to contain at least 71 million ounces of gold.

Bre-X's Indonesian partners and their partners would get 30 percent, the government 10 percent and U.S. company Freeport McMoRan Copper and Gold Inc 15 percent. Freeport will develop and operate the mine.

Sudjana said Bre-X and its partners in Busang had applied for contracts of work covering Busang II and Busang III. Bre-X already had a contract of work for Busang I with a different Indonesian partner.
Kuntoro said the government would soon approve 68 outstanding sixth generation contracts of work (COWS) for the mining industry.
He said the approval of the COWS, which had been expected last year, had nothing to do with Bre-X.
"Furthermore, we will enter the seventh generation in which we will stress community development in mining. How mining activities are to benefit the people around," Kuntoro said.
The sixth generation COWS is mainly intended to accommodate provisions of a 1995 tax law which reduces corporate tax for mining investors to a maximum of 30 percent from the previous 35 percent.
Kuntoro said there were 300 COW application in the pipeline covering mineral and coal explorations.
